chunks: And with this chain of narration, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), he said:
"The testimony of the one who has performed Hajj (Sābiq al-Hajj) is not accepted, because he killed his mount, consumed his provisions, exhausted his self, and slighted his prayer."
I asked: "What about the renter (Mukārī), the camel driver (al-Jammāl), and the sailor (al-Mallāḥ)?" He said: "There is no harm with them; their testimony is accepted if they are virtuous (Ṣulḥāʾ)."

key_terms.الْجَمَّالُ: Al-Jammāl: A camel driver or carrier.
key_terms.الْمُكَارِي: Al-Mukārī: One who rents out animals or vehicles for transport.
key_terms.سَابِقُ الْحَاجِّ: Sābiq al-Hajj: A pilgrim who performs Hajj alone or with few companions, bearing all expenses and duties himself.
key_terms.شَهَادَةٌ: Shahādah: Testimony or witness testimony in legal contexts.
key_terms.صُلَحَاءَ: Ṣulḥāʾ: Plural of ṣalūḥ, meaning virtuous, pious, or upright individuals.

ai.seo_question: Why is the testimony of a Sābiq al-Hajj not accepted in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* to distinguish between the spiritual negligence of the self-focused pilgrim, who neglects prayer and exhausts himself, and the professional service providers like drivers and sailors, whose testimony is valid if they are *ṣulḥāʾ* (virtuous/upright). This highlights the Shia juristic principle that physical exertion or travel alone does not invalidate testimony, but rather the specific neglect of religious duties and moral integrity does.
